claims.text: What the image looks like Hot nose on cerebral perfusion scan = brain death sign
claims.quote: 'Hot nose' on cerebral perfusion scan = brain death sign

claims.text: Flow study (with items 2–7 confirmed, when components of the examination or apnea testing cannot be completed or results are uncertain): conventional angiography, transcranial Doppler ultrasonography (adults only; not yet validated in children), or technetium-99m hexamethylpropyleneamine oxime brain scanning shows no intracranial blood flow
claims.quote: c. Items 2–7 have been confirmed AND (done when components of the examination or apnea testing cannot be completed or when results of the examination are uncertain) Conventional angiography, transcranial Doppler ultrasonography (to be used only in adults; not yet validated in children), or technetium-99m hexamethylpropyleneamine oxime brain scanning shows no intracranial blood flow.

claims.text: EEG alternative (same situation): an EEG shows electrocortical silence
claims.quote: b. Items 2–7 have been confirmed AND (done when components of the examination or apnea testing cannot be completed or when results of the examination are uncertain) An EEG shows electrocortical silence.

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) Diagnosis: serial determination of clinical criteria showing permanent loss of brain function, including that of the brain stem; apnea testing; sometimes EEG, brain vascular imaging, or both
claims.quote: Serial determination of clinical criteria to demonstrate permanent loss of brain function, including that of the brain stem Apnea testing Sometimes electroencephalography (EEG), brain vascular imaging, or both

claims.text: EEG or brain perfusion tests are sometimes used to confirm absence of brain activity or blood flow but are not usually required; they are indicated when apnea testing is not hemodynamically tolerated and when only 1 neurologic examination is desirable (eg, to expedite organ procurement for transplantation)
claims.quote: Sometimes EEG or tests of brain perfusion are used to confirm absence of brain activity or brain blood flow and thus provide additional evidence to family members, but these tests are not usually required. They are indicated when apnea testing is not hemodynamically tolerated and when only 1 neurologic examination is desirable (eg, to expedite organ procurement for transplantation).

claims.text: Required before declaring: a known catastrophic and permanent brain injury; a structural or metabolic cause of brain damage; use of potentially anesthetizing or paralyzing medications and illicit drugs excluded; potentially reversible metabolic abnormalities (including hypoglycemia and acid-base and electrolyte abnormalities) excluded
claims.quote: For a clinician to declare brain death (see table ) (1), the following requirements must be met: A known catastrophic and permanent brain injury must have occurred. A structural or metabolic cause of brain damage must be present. Use of potentially anesthetizing (including nervous system depressants and alcohol) or paralyzing medications and illicit drugs, especially self-administered, must be excluded. Potentially reversible metabolic abnormalities, including hypoglycemia and acid-base and electrolyte abnormalities, must be excluded.

claims.text: Assessment should not begin until at least 24 hours after a brain injury capable of causing brain death; if hypothermia is present, a core temperature < 36° C must be increased slowly to > 36° C for ≥ 24 hours; systolic blood pressure should be ≥ 100 mm Hg and mean arterial pressure maintained at ≥ 75 mm Hg
claims.quote: Brain death assessment should not begin until at least 24 hours after a brain injury capable of causing brain death. If hypothermia is present, a core temperature < 36° C must be increased slowly to > 36° C for ≥ 24 hours. Systolic blood pressure should be ≥ 100 mm Hg, and mean arterial pressure should be maintained at ≥ 75 mm Hg.

claims.text: Examination includes pupil reactivity, oculovestibular, oculocephalic and corneal reflexes, and apnea testing
claims.quote: Examination includes Assessment of pupil reactivity Assessment of oculovestibular, oculocephalic, and corneal reflexes Apnea testing

claims.text: Apnea test: despite the passively rising PaCO2, brain death requires the absence of spontaneous respirations, a pH of < 7.30, and a PaCO2 of ≥ 60 mm Hg and ≥ 20 mm Hg above the patient's baseline
claims.quote: Despite the ventilatory stimulus of the passively rising PaCO2, brain death requires the absence of spontaneous respirations, a pH of < 7.30, and a PaCO2 of ≥ 60 mm Hg and ≥ 20 mm Hg above the patient's baseline.

claims.text: Adults: at least 1 complete assessment must be done, and at least 1 additional examination by the same or another independent clinician is recommended to reduce the risk of a false-positive assessment; for children, some states advise 2 separate examinations by independent clinicians separated by at least 48 hours
claims.quote: At least 1 complete brain death assessment by a clinician must be done for an adult, but doing at least 1 additional brain death examination subsequently by the same or another independent clinician is recommended to reduce the risk of a false-positive assessment. For children, some states advise clinicians to do 2 separate examinations by independent clinicians separated by at least 48 hours (1).

claims.text: Causes Ventilators and medications can perpetuate cardiopulmonary and other body functions despite complete cessation of all cerebral activity; total cessation of integrated brain function, especially that of the brain stem, is accepted legally and culturally in most of the world as a person's death
claims.quote: The concept of brain death developed because ventilators and medications can perpetuate cardiopulmonary and other body functions despite complete cessation of all cerebral activity. The determination that brain death/death by neurologic criteria (ie, total cessation of integrated brain function, especially that of the brain stem) constitutes a person’s death has been accepted legally and culturally in most of the world.

claims.text: Symptoms Brain death is not declared or assessed if the patient is breathing spontaneously, can be aroused, is not in coma, or has intact brain stem reflexes
claims.quote: Brain death should not be declared or considered and brain death assessment should not be done if any of the following is present: The patient is breathing spontaneously. The patient can be aroused. The patient is not in coma. The patient has intact brain stem reflexes.

claims.text: During terminal apnea, spinal motor reflexes may occur (arching of the back, neck turning, stiffening of the legs, upper extremity flexion: the so-called Lazarus sign); family members who wish to be present when the ventilator is shut off need to be warned
claims.quote: Spinal motor reflexes may occur during terminal apnea; they include arching of the back, neck turning, stiffening of the legs, and upper extremity flexion (the so-called Lazarus sign). Family members who wish to be present when the ventilator is shut off need to be warned of such reflex movements.

claims.text: Treatment and next step The diagnosis of brain death is equivalent to the person's death; after confirmation, all supporting cardiac and respiratory treatments are ended, and cessation of ventilatory support results in terminal arrhythmias
claims.quote: The diagnosis of brain death is equivalent to the person’s death. After brain death is confirmed, all supporting cardiac and respiratory treatments are ended. Cessation of ventilatory support results in terminal arrhythmias.

claims.text: Before the examination, the family or caregivers should be informed of the process and offered the opportunity to witness the evaluation, which may help them accept that brain death has occurred
claims.quote: Before the examination for brain death, the patient's family or caregivers should be informed of the process and be offered the opportunity to witness the brain death evaluation process, which may help them accept that brain death has occurred.
